misconception: Claude reads minds — it doesn't need specific instructions to give you what you actually want.

mentorLessons.line: Show your prompt to a colleague with zero context. If they'd be confused, so will Claude. Specificity beats cleverness every time.
Tell Claude *why* you're asking and *what* the answer is for. The reasoning target sharpens the answer.
A few well-built examples cut ambiguity faster than any amount of description. Show, don't just tell.
Say exactly what shape you want the answer in — bullets, a table, JSON, plain prose. Claude won't guess your preferred format.
For a complex prompt, wrap parts in tags like <context> and <instructions>. It stops your intent from blurring together.
When accuracy matters, ask Claude to reason step by step out loud. Errors surface when the thinking is visible.
A brand-new chat remembers nothing from an unrelated past chat. Only a Project — or content you paste in — carries context forward.
Chat is a single ephemeral conversation. A Project is a persistent workspace. Claude Code is agentic — it writes and runs things itself.

questions.prompt: Your prompt keeps getting generic answers. Best first fix?
choices: Add specifics: context, format, an example
questions.reteach: Specificity beats repetition — give context, the format you want, and an example.
hardChoices: Start with a role like 'You are an expert' — the role alone sharpens output
Rewrite it as one short direct question so nothing distracts from the ask
Ask Claude to critique its answer, then resend the same prompt unchanged

questions.prompt: "Write a poem" gets a bland result. What's the better prompt?
choices: "Write a 4-line rhyming poem about a forgotten library, noir tone"
"You are a poet, write a poem"
questions.reteach: Concrete details — length, subject, tone — replace guesswork with direction.
hardChoices: "Write a poem in the style of a famous poet"
"You are an award-winning poet. Write a poem"
"Write a poem, and make it vivid, evocative, and emotionally powerful"

questions.prompt: You want a customer email about a service outage. What strengthens the prompt most?
choices: Explaining who it's for and what it needs to accomplish
questions.reteach: Context — audience and purpose — lets Claude tailor tone, depth, and format correctly.
hardChoices: Pasting the full incident postmortem so Claude has every technical detail
Adding 'use a formal, apologetic tone' — tone direction covers the rest
Requesting three draft variants so you can choose the best one

questions.prompt: True or false: fewer words in a prompt always means a faster, better answer.
questions.reteach: Brevity without context just forces Claude to guess your intent.
hardChoices: True — shorter prompts leave less room for Claude to get confused
False — longer is always better; every added word improves the answer
True for simple factual lookups, false only for multi-step tasks

questions.prompt: You need Claude to match a very specific writing style. Most reliable approach?
choices: Provide 2-3 example passages in that style
Ask Claude to guess your style
questions.reteach: Concrete examples cut ambiguity far more than adjectives ever can.
hardChoices: Describe its traits precisely: sentence length, vocabulary, rhythm
Name a well-known author it resembles and let Claude infer the rest
Ask Claude to ask you clarifying questions about the style first

questions.prompt: How many well-built examples typically helps most for a tricky format?
choices: As many as physically possible, always
questions.reteach: A handful of clear examples is usually the sweet spot — enough to show the pattern without burying it.
hardChoices: Exactly one — a single canonical example avoids mixed signals
Ten or more — accuracy keeps climbing with every example you add
None, if the description is precise — examples are only a fallback

questions.prompt: You need the output as a JSON array, but you don't say so. What happens?
choices: Claude may guess the wrong format entirely
It's automatically detected from context every time
questions.reteach: State the exact output format — Claude won't reliably infer it from an unspecified request.
hardChoices: Claude will use JSON but may invent its own field names and nesting
Claude reliably asks a clarifying question before picking a format
Claude defaults to a markdown table for anything list-shaped

questions.prompt: Best way to lock in an exact output shape?
choices: State it explicitly (e.g. a table, JSON) or show an example of it
Ask twice in the same message
questions.reteach: Explicit format instructions — or a worked example — remove the guesswork.
hardChoices: Give a role like 'You are a JSON generator' and trust it from there
Ask for 'a structured format' and let Claude fill in the details
Fix formatting with follow-up messages instead of specifying upfront

questions.prompt: Your prompt has background info, instructions, and sample data all mixed together. What helps most?
choices: Separating them with tags like <context> and <instructions>
Making it all one giant sentence
questions.reteach: Structure tags stop different parts of a complex prompt from blurring together.
hardChoices: Splitting it into three separate messages sent one after another
Moving every instruction to the very end so it's read last
Cutting the background info — instructions alone usually suffice

questions.prompt: True or false: structure tags like <example> are only useful for programmers.
choices: True — regular prompts don't need them
False — anyone writing a complex prompt benefits
False, but only in Claude Code
questions.reteach: Structure tags help any complex prompt, technical or not — they clarify where one part ends and another begins.
hardChoices: True — tags are parsed as code, so they only help technical prompts
False, but they only pay off once a prompt is thousands of words long
True in the API; the chat interface strips them out

questions.prompt: A task needs careful accuracy (like multi-step math or logic). What should you ask for?
choices: Explicit step-by-step reasoning before the final answer
questions.reteach: Asking Claude to reason step by step surfaces errors that a jump-to-the-answer response would hide.
hardChoices: Ask twice and compare — matching answers prove correctness
Ask for a short, confident answer so Claude commits to one result
Ask Claude to verify its answer after it has already given it

questions.prompt: Why does asking Claude to "think out loud" often improve accuracy?
choices: It doesn't — it just uses more tokens
Visible reasoning surfaces mistakes before the final answer locks in
It's only useful for creative writing
questions.reteach: When reasoning is visible, errors in logic become spottable — and fixable — before the answer is final.
hardChoices: Longer responses get more compute, so extra words add accuracy
It slows generation down, and slower output is inherently more careful
It only helps you follow along — the answer itself is unchanged

questions.prompt: You mentioned a preference in a chat last week. You open a new, unrelated chat today. Does Claude remember it?
choices: No — a new chat doesn't carry over an unrelated past conversation
questions.reteach: A fresh chat starts fresh — carrying context forward needs a Project, or you re-supplying it.
hardChoices: Only if both chats live inside the same Project
Only if the old chat is recent enough to still be in the context window
Yes, but only preferences you stated as explicit instructions

questions.prompt: How do you make sure Claude has your team's persistent context in every chat?
choices: Put it in a Project so it's available across every chat inside it
questions.reteach: Projects hold persistent context across every chat inside them — no re-explaining needed.
hardChoices: Keep one long-running chat for everything so context never resets
State it once anywhere — Claude folds it into your account settings
Pin the key message in one chat and reference that chat by name later

questions.prompt: What's the real difference between a Chat and a Project?
choices: A Project is a persistent workspace; Chat is a single ephemeral conversation
questions.reteach: Chat is one-off; a Project persists instructions, docs, and context across every chat inside it.
hardChoices: A Project is just a folder for organizing chats, with no shared context
Chats inside a Project share one live context window in real time
Projects run a more capable model than standalone chats

questions.prompt: Which mode is agentic — writing and running things itself rather than just replying?
questions.reteach: Claude Code is agentic — it can write and execute actions, not just produce text back to you.
hardChoices: Projects — they execute their custom instructions autonomously
Chat, once extended thinking is switched on
Any mode becomes agentic once you upload a file to work on
